item.title: MAGA’s Self-Destructive Culture War
item.description: Polls suggest that MAGA fanaticism might not be playing so well outside US President Donald Trump’s loyal base. But if the Democrats want to retake one or both chambers of Congress, they should concentrate on the economy and not answer Republican extremism with a culture war of their own.

item.title: How to Break the German Malaise
item.description: For too long, Germany’s political and corporate elite coasted on the country’s postwar economic and political success story, avoiding difficult but necessary reforms that could have kept extremist populist parties at bay. Now that the barbarians are at the gates, mainstream elites must rethink everything.

item.title: Europe’s Place in the Global Redivision of Labor
item.description: While the US continues to lead in software, some high-tech sectors, and hydrocarbons, China is becoming increasingly competitive in many high-tech, capital-intensive sectors, not least those once dominated by Europe. The EU does have a relative advantage in this new economic order, if only its leaders would recognize it.

item.title: The World Has Passed Peak Trump
item.description: US President Donald Trump, previously the most powerful, unpredictable force on the international stage, has now passed the peak of his ability to disrupt the international order. With his approval ratings collapsing, foreign leaders whose tenures will extend beyond his own are starting to write him off.

item.title: Global Financial Reform that Centers African Women
item.description: While gender-equality objectives often fall by the wayside in times of upheaval, the current rupture in the multilateral order creates an opportunity to build a debt architecture that will deliver for the women of Africa. The first steps toward this goal can be taken at this month’s IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.

item.title: How Africa Can Leverage the US-China Thaw
item.description: As dollar borrowing costs soar, Chinese rates are approaching record lows. This divergence, combined with the US-China thaw, creates an opportunity for African governments: partner with the US on gas and with China on solar and storage, and tap lower-cost Asian capital markets to finance investments in both.

item.title: Closing NATO’s Deterrence Gap
item.description: With Russian provocations against NATO member states growing more frequent, the alliance urgently needs to develop a credible doctrine of punitive deterrence to guide its response to acts of aggression that fall below the threshold of war. Mere territorial defense is not enough.

item.title: The India-Pakistan Cold War
item.description: The current stalemate between India and Pakistan should be viewed not as a pause between rounds of negotiation, but rather as part of a deliberate Indian strategy of disengagement. India will return to the negotiating table only after Pakistan dismantles, comprehensively and verifiably, its state-supported terrorist networks.

item.title: The Next Era of Reform Must Be About Capability
item.description: Economic development should no longer be measured solely by how much finance is mobilized or how much fiscal space is created. It must also be judged by whether countries emerge more capable of setting their own priorities, responding to challenges, and seizing new opportunities to shape their own future.

item.title: With AI, Sharing Is Caring
item.description: Although the public's distrust of Big Tech is understandable, given past experience, that is not a reason to starve AI models of the information and data they will need to be useful. If serving the public interest is the goal, everyone relying on the technology's output has a duty to provide high-quality input.

item.title: Why the US-China Trade Truce Matters
item.description: Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump’s agreement to extend their trade truce reflects the fact that both sides have leverage over the other. In a world where the rules-based trading system is not functioning, the current fragile equilibrium may be the best one can hope for.

item.title: Brazil’s Voters Have Moved
item.description: A strong performance by the right-wing, Donald Trump-aligned candidate in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election demonstrates that the left-wing ruling party has failed to keep up with the times. The Brazilian electorate is older, more devout, and more preoccupied with crime and personal security than it once was.

item.title: Does Inclusive Finance Really Need Stablecoins?
item.description: Today, 1.3 billion adults—more than half of them women—remain excluded from the formal financial system, and lower-income consumers still struggle to find and access the financial products and services they need. Contrary to much hype, stablecoins are not the best way to solve either of these problems.

item.title: Brazil’s Election Debacle Is Lula’s Fault
item.description: Brazil's left has just suffered a crushing election defeat and will most likely lose the presidency at the end of October. The causes are many, beginning with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's longstanding refusal to groom an appealing successor.

item.title: Sino-American Stability Without Trust
item.description: The main outcomes of the Trump-Xi summit—the two-month trade extension, the dialogue on AI, and even the carefully chosen language on Taiwan—point to Sino-American relations being in a holding pattern. For both sides, the main task is to prevent managed rivalry from devolving into outright confrontation.

item.title: Iran’s Moment of Opportunity
item.description: America and Israel's unilateral aggression against Iran lacked international legitimacy and predictably destabilized the entire region. But as justified as the Iranian leadership might feel in pursuing an obstinately maximalist strategy, it must be careful not to mistake short-term advantages for longer-term gains.

item.title: Is Russia’s Placement on the Security Council Legal?
item.description: When Russia replaced the Soviet Union as a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council in 1991, it did not even attempt to follow the process outlined in the UN Charter. Now that Russia’s usurpation of the USSR’s seat has enabled it to wage a war of aggression, the dubious legal status of its position must be revisited.

item.title: To Support Nepal, Waive Remittance Fees
item.description: To help Nepal move from rescue and relief toward reconstruction, money-transfer companies and banks ought to waive fees on remittances sent to the country for at least two months. Doing so could provide additional relief totaling several times more than what a recent emergency appeal by the United Nations generated.

item.title: What a Canada–Europe Alliance Needs
item.description: With trade, finance, technology, and supply chains having all become instruments of coercion, Canada, Europe, and other likeminded democracies must come together to defend their interests. But strategic convergence between governments is not enough; if a new alliance is to endure, it needs deep roots in society.

item.title: Trump’s Great Oil Heist
item.description: Venezuela’s hopes for a democratic transition are fading as the US works to take control of its vast oil wealth. Billions in US and foreign investment could strengthen the chavista regime and give future American presidents powerful incentives to preserve the political status quo.
